warmup.q: @JvmInline value class Money(val cents: Long). Which of these creates a Money object on the heap at run time?
options: val total = a + b, where a and b are Money
class Invoice(val amount: Money) when you build an Invoice
None of them: a value class is never boxed
warmup.why: A List holds objects, so each element is boxed into a real Money (the compiler calls Money.box-impl(long)). Inside Invoice the property is stored as a long field, and a + b compiles to a static method on two longs. The last option is the common belief, and the docs say the opposite: value classes are boxed whenever they are used as another type.

sections.h: A value class is a type at compile time and a long at run time
sections.html:
A Long parameter named amountMinor will accept an order id without complaint. Both are Long, so the compiler can't tell them apart. The classic fix is a small wrapper class, class Cents(val value: Long), and it works, but every amount is now an extra object on the heap. Kotlin's value class keeps the wrapper's type safety and, wherever it can, drops the object: at run time only the wrapped value, the underlying type (Long here), is left. Here is the wrapper in both languages:

Java
// Java's closest shape today: a record. It's a real object, allocated on every new.
record Cents(long value) {
    Cents {
        if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + value);
    }
}
Kotlin
@JvmInline
value class Cents(val value: Long) {
    init {
        require(value >= 0) { "negative amount: $value" }
    }

    operator fun plus(other: Cents): Cents = Cents(value + other.value)

    override fun toString(): String = "$value cents"
}

fun charge(amount: Cents): String = "charged $amount"

charge(199L)   // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Long', but 'Cents' was expected.

The rules are short. On the JVM you write @JvmInline value class with exactly one property in the primary constructor. You may add init blocks, functions, secondary constructors and properties without backing fields (so no lateinit and no delegation). A value class can implement interfaces, can't extend a class, and is always final.

At run time most of it disappears. javap -p on the demo shows what the compiler built:

public static final java.lang.String charge-X49TzF8(long);   // takes a plain long
public static long constructor-impl(long);                  // Cents(...) runs init here
public static final long plus-dpzqtSM(long, long);          // a member, now static on longs
public static final Cents box-impl(long);                   // used only when a box is needed

Cents(150) compiles to a call to constructor-impl, which runs your init block and returns the same long. No object is created. plus turned into a static method that adds two longs. The Cents class still exists, with one long field, for the moments when a real object is needed. That's the next section.

Compare a type alias. typealias CentsAlias = Long gives you a second name and nothing else: the docs say aliases are assignment-compatible with their underlying type, and value classes are not. In the demo, an orderId: Long goes straight into chargeAlias and compiles. Use aliases to shorten long generic types. Use value classes where mixing up two values would be a bug.

You already use value classes from the standard library: UInt, ULong, kotlin.time.Duration and kotlin.Result are all declared this way, and javap shows the same box-impl and unbox-impl on each.

video.title: A value class is its own type to the compiler and a plain long at run time, boxed whenever it is used as another type

sections.h: Boxed whenever it is used as another type
sections.html:
Value classes do get boxed, which means wrapped in a real Money object on the heap, the way Java wraps a long in a Long. The rule fits in one line of the docs: inline classes are boxed whenever they are used as another type.

Java
// Java's long and Long follow the same rule: a primitive where it can, a box when it must
static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; }

long minor = 1_999;
Object boxed = asGeneric(minor);      // autoboxed into a Long object
List<Long> list = List.of(minor);     // another Long object
Kotlin
fun <T> asGeneric(x: T): Any? = x     // used as T: boxed
fun asNullable(a: Amount?): Any? = a  // used as Amount?: boxed
fun asInterface(p: Priced): Any = p   // used as Priced: boxed

class Invoice(val amount: Amount)     // used as Amount: stored as a long field

Four cases box: a generic type parameter, a nullable type (Amount? must be able to hold null, and a long can't), an interface the class implements, and anything typed Any, which includes every collection and println. In the bytecode each one shows up as a call to Amount.box-impl(long) right before the call that needs the object. So a List<Money> holds one Money object per element. The docs draw the same comparison you'd draw: it's like Int being either a primitive int or a java.lang.Integer.

Equality still works by value. a == Amount(1_999) compiles to equals-impl0(long, long), a comparison of two longs. Identity doesn't exist: a === b is a compile error, identity equality for arguments of types 'Amount' and 'Amount' is prohibited. That's stricter than Java, where Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; a == b is false and the same code with 100L is true, because small boxes are cached.

In practice, a value class saves the allocation wherever it's used as itself: fields, parameters, return values, arithmetic. That covers most domain code. A hot path that pushes millions of amounts through a List<Money> or a generic Map pays the same boxing as List<Long>. If that shows up in a profile, use a LongArray, as you would in Java.

alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l02.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of BoxingDemo.kt. Java has the same split for long and Long: a primitive where it can, * a box when the value is used as a generic type, a nullable, or Object. Kotlin forbids === on * value classes; Java lets you compare boxes by identity, and it goes wrong above 127. */ public class BoxingDemoJava { static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; } public static void main(String[] args) { long minor = 1_999; Object boxed = asGeneric(minor); // autoboxed to Long System.out.println("as Object: " + boxed.getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("in a list: " + List.of(minor).get(0).getClass().getSimpleName()); Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; System.out.println("a == b (identity): " + (a == b)); // two different Long objects System.out.println("a.equals(b): " + a.equals(b)); Long small1 = 100L, small2 = 100L; System.out.println("100L == 100L: " + (small1 == small2)); // cached box, so true } }

try.expect: The field in Invoice is a long. Every other line prints Amount, because generic, nullable, interface and list uses all box, and javap shows four box-impl calls in main, one before each of those calls. The equality line prints true through equals-impl0. The wrong move fails with identity equality for arguments of types 'Amount' and 'Amount' is prohibited. The Java twin prints false for a == b with 1,999 and true with 100: that's the Long cache, a trap Kotlin closes for value classes.

sections.h: Mangled names keep Java out, and @JvmName lets it back in
sections.html:
Look at that name again: charge-X49TzF8(long). The compiler adds a hash to every function that takes a value class. The docs call it mangling, and it does two jobs. It prevents clashes: describe(key: IdempotencyKey) and describe(raw: String) would both be describe(String) in the bytecode, and with mangling they become describe-<hash>(String) and describe(String). And it keeps Java away from functions that expect a valid value: a - can't appear in a Java method name.

It reaches further than functions. A class with a value-class property gets a private constructor, plus a public synthetic one with an extra DefaultConstructorMarker parameter, and a mangled getter: the demo's Invoice has getAmount-hwXtt_M(). Java can't build it or read it by name. Members that return a value class are mangled too, so the lab's Money.Companion.parse becomes parse-LC5NfZc(String). A top-level function that only returns one is not: parseAmount(String) hands Java a plain long.

For a single function, the quick fix is @JvmName:

Java
System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.chargeFromJava(199L));   // charged 199 cents
System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.chargeFromJava(-5L));    // charged -5 cents: init never ran
// ValueClassDemoKt.charge(199L);                            // error: cannot find symbol
Kotlin
@JvmName("chargeFromJava")
fun chargeJava(amount: Cents): String = "charged $amount"

Read the second Java line again. Java passes a raw long, and nothing runs init on the way in. @JvmName opens a door around your validation, so a function meant for Java should validate again, for example by building a fresh Cents(amount.value).

Kotlin 2.2.0 added a fuller answer, @JvmExposeBoxed. It is still Experimental in 2.4, so you opt in with @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class). On a class it adds a public constructor that runs init. On a function it adds a version that takes and returns the box, describeFee(Fee), next to the mangled describeFee-pUsR5hI(long). The compiler flag -Xjvm-expose-boxed does the same for a whole module.

Java
Fee fee = new Fee(125);                              // a real constructor: init runs
System.out.println(ExposeBoxedDemoKt.describeFee(fee.doubled()));
Kotlin
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)

@JvmExposeBoxed
@JvmInline
value class Fee(val minor: Long) {
    init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative fee: $minor" } }
    fun doubled(): Fee = Fee(minor * 2)
}

@JvmExposeBoxed
fun describeFee(fee: Fee): String = "fee of ${fee.minor} minor units"

Frameworks see the same bytecode Java does. Anything that finds getters by name through reflection, such as a JSON mapper or an ORM reading an entity, will meet getAmount-hwXtt_M. Check how your libraries handle that before you put value classes in DTOs or entities.

steps: Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.Fee workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ExposeBoxedDemoKt. Find the two doubled methods and the two describeFee methods.

refs.title: Calling Kotlin from Java: inline value classes

sections.html:
Give a value class two properties and the compiler stops you: value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. So Point(x, y) or Money(cents, currency) can't be value classes on the JVM in Kotlin 2.4, and there is no hidden flag for it.

The limit comes from the JVM. Kotlin can erase a one-field class into its field because the JVM already has a long. A two-field value with no identity needs support from the JVM itself, which is Project Valhalla. JEP 401, value classes and objects for Java, is integrated into JDK 28 as a preview feature, and JDK 28 is still in development. The Kotlin team's design notes explain why @JvmInline is mandatory today: it marks the current compile-time trick, so that a plain value class without the annotation can later compile to real Valhalla value classes. They call multi-field value classes before Valhalla "all theoretical". No Kotlin release has a Valhalla mode yet.

For now, the one-field limit shapes your design. An amount that carries its own currency stays a data class. Or you keep the currency elsewhere: many payment services give each account one currency, so the amount needs none of its own.

Where do value classes pay off? IDs and keys (PaymentId, MerchantId, IdempotencyKey), amounts in minor units, and validated strings such as an IBAN: anywhere two Strings or two Longs could be swapped by accident. Validation runs once, in init, and the type is the proof that it ran. Where don't they? In APIs that Java code calls a lot, unless you add @JvmName overloads or @JvmExposeBoxed, and in classes that reflection-heavy frameworks read. Keep them in the Kotlin domain code and convert at the edges.

try.title: Try a second field
steps: In ValueClassDemo.kt, change value class Cents(val value: Long) to value class Cents(val value: Long, val currency: String). Run the demo.
Undo it. Which of your own types would you make a value class, and which would stay a data class?
try.expect: The build fails with value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. Single-value concepts such as ids, keys and minor-unit amounts fit. Anything with two parts (amount plus currency, a card's expiry month and year) stays a data class for now.

analogy: A value class is a label the compiler checks and then peels off. Inside Kotlin, the label Money stops you from putting an order id in the amount slot. At run time the label is gone and only the number travels, except when the number has to go somewhere that only takes objects, like a list. Then the compiler packs it in a box with the label printed on the outside. The analogy breaks at the border with Java: Java can't read the label at all, so it either can't call the function, or, through @JvmName, hands in a bare number that nobody checked.
world: Payment code is full of values that share a JVM type and must never be mixed. paymentId, merchantId and idempotencyKey are all String; amountMinor, feeMinor and createdAtEpochMs are all Long. One value class per concept turns a swapped argument in refund(merchantId, paymentId) into a compile error, with no allocation in Kotlin code. Keep them in the domain and service layers of your Quarkus service. At the edges, look at what reads them: a REST DTO with val amount: Money has a getter named getAmount-<hash> in the bytecode, and the Java modules your team still maintains can't call a mangled function until you add @JvmName or @JvmExposeBoxed.
mistake:
Believing a value class is never boxed, and then counting on it in a hot path that goes through generics. A Map<PaymentId, Money> or a List<Money> holds a boxed object per entry, exactly like List<Long>, and a nullable Money? field holds a reference to a box:

Java
List<Long> amounts = new ArrayList<>();
for (long m : rawAmounts) amounts.add(m);          // one Long object per element
Kotlin
val amounts = ArrayList<Money>()
for (m in rawAmounts) amounts += Money(m)         // one Money object per element

The value class still gives you type safety in those places, just not the allocation savings. Profile before you rely on them, and use a primitive array (LongArray) for large numeric batches.

compare.title: An idempotency key: Java record vs Kotlin value class

java.title: IdempotencyKey.java
java.html: public record IdempotencyKey(String value) { public IdempotencyKey { if (value.length() < 8 || value.length() > 64) throw new IllegalArgumentException("idempotency key must be 8 to 64 characters"); if (!value.matches("[A-Za-z0-9_-]+")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad character in idempotency key: " + value); } } // every new IdempotencyKey(...) is an object with identity static Charge findCharge(IdempotencyKey key) { ... } // JVM: findCharge(IdempotencyKey)

kotlin.title: IdempotencyKey.kt
kotlin.html: @JvmInline value class IdempotencyKey(val value: String) { init { require(value.length in 8..64) { "idempotency key must be 8 to 64 characters" } require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Za-z0-9_-]+"))) { "bad character in idempotency key: $value" } } } // IdempotencyKey(...) runs init and returns the same String fun findCharge(key: IdempotencyKey): Charge? = TODO() // JVM: findCharge-<hash>(String)

compare.note: Both validate once at construction and both compare by value. The record is a real object: each new allocates, and a map keyed by it holds those objects. The value class is a String at run time wherever it is used as itself, so findCharge costs exactly what a String parameter costs. The price is on the Java side: Java sees findCharge-<hash>(String), which it can't call, and can't construct an IdempotencyKey at all without @JvmExposeBoxed. JEP 401, a preview in JDK 28, adds value record to Java: a record without identity, which gives the JVM room to flatten it.

worked.title: Make a swapped argument a compile error, then give Java a safe door

steps.say: A refund call takes two Strings and a Long. Someone swapped the ids in a hotfix, and it compiled.
steps.code: static String refund(String merchantId, String paymentId, long amountMinor) { ... } refund(paymentId, merchantId, 1_999); // swapped: compiles, refunds the wrong thing

alt.html: fun refund(merchantId: String, paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long): String = TODO() refund(paymentId, merchantId, 1_999) // swapped: compiles, refunds the wrong thing

steps.say: Give each concept its own value class. The swapped call now fails to compile, twice, and nothing allocates: in the bytecode the function still takes two Strings and a long.
steps.code: @JvmInline value class MerchantId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class Money(val cents: Long) // 1. one type per concept fun refund(merchant: MerchantId, payment: PaymentId, amount: Money): String = TODO() refund(payment, merchant, Money(1_999)) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'PaymentId', but 'MerchantId' was expected. // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MerchantId', but 'PaymentId' was expected.

alt.html: // Java gets the same safety from records, at the cost of an object each record MerchantId(String value) {} record PaymentId(String value) {} static String refund(MerchantId merchant, PaymentId payment, long amountMinor) { ... } refund(payment, merchant, 1_999); // error: incompatible types: PaymentId cannot be converted to MerchantId

steps.say: Check the Java view. javap shows refund-<hash>(String, String, long): the Java module that also issues refunds can't call it any more. Don't reach for @JvmName here, because Java would pass raw values past every init. Add a Java entry point that takes the raw types and builds the value classes, so validation runs.
steps.code: // 2. a door for Java: raw types in, value classes (and their init blocks) inside fun refundFromJava(merchantId: String, paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long): String = refund(MerchantId(merchantId), PaymentId(paymentId), Money(amountMinor)) // javap: refund-<hash>(String, String, long) and refundFromJava(String, String, long)

alt.html: // 3. the Java module calls the plain name; a negative amount fails inside Money's init String result = RefundsKt.refundFromJava("m-981", "pay_7", 1_999L);

steps.say: Java can still swap the two strings in refundFromJava, so the door is a compromise: it validates values, it can't check names. That's why the type safety belongs in Kotlin and the door belongs at the edge, used by as few callers as possible.

lab.title: Money and IdempotencyKey value classes with validation
steps: Run the tests. All nine fail.
In Money.kt, add the init block (TODO 1), then write plus, times, compareTo, toString and parse (TODOs 2 to 5).
In IdempotencyKey.kt, add the init block (TODO 6): 8 to 64 characters, ASCII letters, digits, - and _ only.

Run the tests until all nine pass. Then run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/main workbench.kotlin.l02.ReceiptsKt and match each name to the Kotlin function it came from.
hints: init { require(cents >= 0) { "amount must be non-negative, was $cents" } } goes inside the class body.
BigDecimal("1.234").setScale(2) throws ArithmeticException: Rounding necessary. That's what you want, so don't pass a rounding mode.
For ASCII only, test it in 'a'..'z' || it in 'A'..'Z' || it in '0'..'9' || it == '-' || it == '_'. isLetterOrDigit() alone also accepts letters such as é.
TODO 7: @JvmName("receiptLineForJava") fun receiptLineJava(amount: Money): String = receiptLine(Money(amount.cents)). Building a new Money calls constructor-impl, which runs init.

Keep override fun toString(): String with its explicit return type. Kotlin 2.4.21 (and 2.3.21) crash with Backend Internal error: Exception during IR lowering when a value class's toString() infers its type from a Java call such as toPlainString() and the value is then used in a string template.

drill.title: Write a validated Iban from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write @JvmInline value class Iban(val value: String) that rejects anything other than 15 to 34 characters of capital letters and digits starting with two letters. Then write the Java record version. Which one allocates when you call send(to: Iban) with it, and what is the JVM name of send in each language?

answer.html: @JvmInline value class Iban(val value: String) { init { require(value.length in 15..34) { "IBAN must be 15 to 34 characters" } require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Z]{2}[A-Z0-9]+"))) { "bad IBAN: $value" } } } fun send(to: Iban): Unit = TODO() // JVM: send-<hash>(String); no object is created

alt.title: Iban.java
alt.html: public record Iban(String value) { public Iban { if (value.length() < 15 || value.length() > 34) throw new IllegalArgumentException("IBAN must be 15 to 34 characters"); if (!value.matches("[A-Z]{2}[A-Z0-9]+")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad IBAN: " + value); } } static void send(Iban to) { } // JVM: send(Iban); every new Iban(...) is an object

recap: @JvmInline value class X(val v: T) has one property, validates in init, is its own type in Kotlin and a plain T in the bytecode wherever it's used as itself.
It is boxed whenever it's used as another type: a generic T, a nullable X?, an interface, Any, and so every collection.
Functions that take a value class get mangled JVM names such as charge-X49TzF8(long). That avoids overload clashes and keeps Java out.
@JvmName lets Java call such a function, but Java passes the raw value and skips init, so validate again. @JvmExposeBoxed (Experimental, opt-in) gives Java a constructor that runs init.
A type alias is only a second name. A value class is a new type.
Only one field on the JVM. Multi-field value classes wait for Valhalla, and JEP 401 is a preview in JDK 28.

explain.prompt: A teammate who mostly writes Java asks why fun charge(m: Money) costs no allocation but List<Money> does, and why their Java code can't call charge. Explain both in your own words.
explain.answer: A value class exists for the compiler, not for the JVM. Where the code uses a Money as a Money (a parameter, a field, a return value), the compiler passes the long inside it, so charge really takes a long and nothing is allocated. A List holds objects, so when a Money goes into one, the compiler has to wrap the long in a real Money object first, the same way Java wraps a long in a Long. That's boxing, and it happens whenever the value is used as another type: generic, nullable, interface or Any. Java can't call charge because the compiler mangles its name to something like charge-X49TzF8(long). The hash avoids clashes with a charge(Long) overload and keeps unchecked longs out. To let Java in, add a function with @JvmName, or one that takes a raw Long and builds the Money itself, so the validation in init still runs.

deeper.html:
Two details that matter when you design with value classes.

A value class can wrap a generic type: @JvmInline value class Box<T>(val value: T). The docs say the underlying type is then mapped to Any?, or to the upper bound of T, so at run time it's an Object field and you rarely save anything. Generic value classes help for type safety, not for speed.

The second detail is a compiler bug worth knowing about. In Kotlin 2.4.21 (and 2.3.21) this crashes the compiler with Backend Internal error: Exception during IR lowering and a NoSuchElementException from the string-concatenation lowering:

@JvmInline value class M(val c: Long) { override fun toString() = java.math.BigDecimal.valueOf(c, 2).toPlainString() }
fun f(m: M) = "x $m"

The trigger is the inferred return type: toPlainString() returns a Java platform type, String!. Write override fun toString(): String = ... and it compiles. It's a small, concrete argument for explicit return types on anything public: they keep platform types from leaking into your API, and here they also keep the compiler alive.

Finally, the history of the keyword, which explains old code you'll still meet. Kotlin 1.5.0 made these classes stable with the value modifier plus @JvmInline on the JVM, and deprecated the old inline class spelling with a warning. The design notes give the reason for the split: @JvmInline names today's erasure trick, which leaves the plain value class free to mean a real Valhalla value class one day.
